topics.observableQuestion: How can a cell double its DNA without doubling its chromosome sets?
topics.learningGoal: Distinguish packaging, genes, chromosomes, homologous sets and sister copies, and interpret a karyotype within its resolution.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Cells store hereditary information in DNA. A copy and a set are different counting units. An image shows features only at its own scale and in its sampled material.

retrieval.prompt: For 2n = 4 after replication, give chromosomes, DNA molecules and sets.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules and two homologous sets.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use a chromosome drawing or karyotype to support one count or structural claim and state a limit on what the image reveals.
criteria: State a resolution or sampling limit.

frames.title: DNA packaging
frames.scenario: A drawing labels a whole chromosome “one gene” and a short DNA region “one chromosome.” Repair the hierarchy.
orderedExplanation: Start with DNA wrapped around associated proteins as chromatin.
Identify a chromosome as one organized DNA molecule with its associated proteins at an unreplicated stage.
Place many gene regions along that DNA rather than equating one region with the whole chromosome.
frames.conclusion: A gene is a region of DNA; a chromosome contains a much longer DNA molecule and many such regions. Packaging changes visibility without creating new genes by itself.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sets and copies
frames.scenario: A model cell has 2n = 4. Count sets, chromosomes and DNA molecules before replication and just after replication.
orderedExplanation: Before replication, identify two sets containing two chromosome types each.
Count four unreplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules.
After replication, keep four chromosomes but count eight sister-chromatid DNA molecules.
frames.conclusion: Before replication: two sets, four chromosomes, four DNA molecules. After replication: two sets, four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Reading karyotypes
frames.scenario: A fictional karyotype contains three copies of one chromosome type and two copies of each remaining autosomal type. What can the image support, and what remains unmeasured?
orderedExplanation: Use the supplied size and banding key to identify the chromosome types.
Count the copies of each type rather than grouping by colour alone.
Report the observed extra copy without inferring a complete sequence or every future trait.
frames.conclusion: The image supports an extra copy of the identified chromosome type in the sampled cell. It does not reveal every DNA variant, all tissues in the organism or a complete developmental outcome.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does an X-shaped chromosome represent two homologues?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. It is one replicated chromosome with joined sister chromatids.

topics.observableQuestion: What can a snapshot of cells reveal about a process unfolding over time?
topics.learningGoal: Track interphase DNA changes, explain control points and calculate conditional duration estimates from supplied population counts.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Replication produces sister copies. A proportion is a part divided by a whole. A snapshot count and a direct time measurement are different kinds of evidence.

retrieval.prompt: What changes during S phase, and what remains unchanged before division?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: DNA amount doubles; chromosome count and homologous-set number remain unchanged.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use the supplied 72/100 interphase count to give a 20-hour-model estimate and one assumption that limits it.
criteria: Identify the synthetic count and model interval.

frames.title: Interphase
frames.scenario: For a model cell with 2n = 6, compare G1, the end of S phase and G2.
orderedExplanation: In G1, record six chromosomes and six DNA molecules.
During S phase, DNA is copied without separating sister centromeres.
At the end of S phase and in G2, record six duplicated chromosomes and twelve DNA molecules.
frames.conclusion: The DNA amount doubles through S phase, while chromosome count and ploidy remain unchanged before division.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Control and division
frames.scenario: A fictional model allows a cell with unrepaired DNA damage to continue into replication and division. Explain one consequence without claiming that every damaged cell becomes a tumour.
orderedExplanation: Identify the checkpoint function that would normally help delay progression.
Trace copying or segregation of damaged genetic material to daughter cells.
Distinguish an increased possibility of abnormal outcomes from an inevitable final disease.
frames.conclusion: Failure of control can allow damaging changes to persist or spread through a lineage. The outcome depends on the change, repair, later controls and the tissue context.

frames.title: Measuring cell populations
frames.scenario: The supplied synthetic count has 72 interphase cells out of 100. Under an explicitly simplified steady-population model with a 20-hour cycle, estimate the interphase duration.
orderedExplanation: Calculate the observed fraction: 72/100 = 0.72.
Multiply by the model cycle length: 0.72 × 20 hours.
State the sampling and steady-population assumptions; these counts were supplied, not obtained from the five authentic example images.
frames.conclusion: The model estimate is 14.4 hours. It is a conditional estimate from a synthetic population count, not a direct timing measurement of one cell.

checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. The count table and authentic stage images are separate evidence sources.

topics.observableQuestion: How do duplicated chromosomes reach two daughter nuclei?
topics.learningGoal: Sequence chromosome changes, explain counting during anaphase and classify authentic cell images from visible features.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: A duplicated chromosome has sister copies. A whole cell and one pole are different counting boundaries. Plant and animal cells form division boundaries differently.

retrieval.prompt: In mitotic anaphase from 2n = 4, count chromosomes in the whole cell and at one pole.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Eight across the still-undivided cell; four at each pole and in each resulting daughter nucleus.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Assign one authentic image to a stage using a visible feature and record any uncertainty in the view.
criteria: Distinguish uncertain image evidence from the ideal diagram.

frames.title: Preparing to separate
frames.scenario: A cell image shows condensed chromosomes, and a later image shows chromosomes arranged near the equatorial plane with spindle attachments. Sequence the observations.
orderedExplanation: Use condensation as evidence consistent with prophase progression.
Use equatorial chromosome alignment and appropriate attachments as evidence of metaphase.
Keep observations about visible structures separate from details too small to resolve in the image.
frames.conclusion: The condensation stage precedes the aligned metaphase arrangement. Stage identification should be justified from the visible structures, not merely a memorized picture position.

frames.title: Separating copies
frames.scenario: A 2n = 4 model cell reaches mitotic anaphase. Count chromosomes in the still-undivided cell and at each pole.
orderedExplanation: Before separation, the cell has four duplicated chromosomes.
When sister centromeres separate, each former chromatid is counted as a chromosome.
Count eight chromosomes across the whole cell, with four moving toward each pole.
frames.conclusion: The whole anaphase cell temporarily contains eight chromosomes by this counting convention; each future daughter nucleus receives four. This is not evidence that each daughter becomes tetraploid.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Finishing cell division
frames.scenario: Compare how a typical animal cell and a typical plant cell divide their cytoplasm after nuclear division.
orderedExplanation: In the animal model, trace constriction of a cleavage furrow.
In the plant model, trace cell-plate formation and development of the separating boundary.
Keep these cytokinesis mechanisms distinct from chromosome separation during mitosis.
frames.conclusion: Both mechanisms partition cytoplasm into daughter cells, but they form the separating boundary differently. Mitosis and cytokinesis are related processes with distinct events.

frames.title: Observation and simulation
frames.scenario: Use the authentic prepared-cell images assigned to this activity. For each proposed stage, name one visible feature before comparing with the supplied stage key.

Record the observed feature before selecting a stage label.
Compare the label with the guide and revise any assignment whose supporting feature is absent or unclear.
frames.conclusion: A defensible answer pairs each stage with image evidence. The supplied synthetic 100-cell table is a separate calculation dataset and must not be described as a count made from these five images.

checkpoint.prompt: Does chromosome condensation alone establish metaphase?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Metaphase requires evidence of the characteristic alignment and attachments.

topics.observableQuestion: Which separation event reduces chromosome sets?
topics.learningGoal: Trace homolog pairing, exchange and two meiotic divisions, comparing them with mitosis using explicit counts.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Homologues carry corresponding loci; sisters are replicated copies. Ploidy counts homologous sets. DNA replicates before the two-division meiotic sequence.

retrieval.prompt: Name what separates in meiosis I and meiosis II.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Meiosis I separates homologues; meiosis II separates sister copies without another S phase.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Follow a 2n = 4 model through both divisions and explain where reduction occurs.
criteria: Keep sister separation and DNA-copy changes distinct.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Pairing and exchange
frames.scenario: In a 2n = 4 model, one homologous pair carries A and a. Show crossing over between nonsister chromatids without exchanging an entire chromosome set.
orderedExplanation: Replicate each homologue before pairing.
Pair corresponding homologues and select one chromatid from each for an exchange at matching regions.
Track the exchanged segments while preserving chromosome number and the overall homologous pair.
frames.conclusion: Crossing over can create new allele combinations along chromatids. It exchanges corresponding DNA regions between nonsister chromatids rather than creating extra sets.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: First meiotic division
frames.scenario: A replicated 2n = 4 cell completes meiosis I. Count chromosomes and sets in one daughter cell and name what separated.
orderedExplanation: Start with two homologous pairs, each chromosome duplicated.
Separate the homologues of each pair while sister chromatids remain joined.
Count two duplicated chromosomes in each product, representing one complete set.
frames.conclusion: Each product is haploid, n = 2, with two duplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules. Homologues, not sister chromatids, separated in this division.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Second meiotic division
frames.scenario: Each product of meiosis I in a 2n = 4 model has two duplicated chromosomes. Describe meiosis II and the final per-cell counts.
orderedExplanation: Begin without another S phase.
Separate sister chromatids in each of the two cells.
Partition the separated chromosomes into four final products, each with one set.
frames.conclusion: Each final product has n = 2: two unduplicated chromosomes and two DNA molecules. Meiosis II separates copies without another reduction in homologous-set number.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Comparing divisions
frames.scenario: Compare mitosis and meiosis for a replicated 2n = 4 starting cell, using products and separation events.
orderedExplanation: Mitosis separates sister copies in one division and normally produces two diploid daughters.
Meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates sister copies.
Count four haploid products after the full meiotic sequence, while retaining the simplified successful-division assumptions.
frames.conclusion: Mitosis normally preserves set number in two products; meiosis reduces it in four products after two divisions. Replication precedes both sequences but occurs only once before the two meiotic divisions.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Is another DNA-replication phase normally inserted between meiosis I and II?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. One replication precedes the two divisions.

topics.observableQuestion: How can variation and chromosome errors arise from the same division sequence?
topics.learningGoal: Compare gamete development, sources of combinations, error timings and twin origins with bounded developmental claims.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates sisters. Gamete content, cytoplasmic size and developmental timing are different features. Fertilization combines two contributions.

retrieval.prompt: Compare the simple meiosis-I and one-cell meiosis-II nondisjunction gamete patterns.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Meiosis I: two n+1 and two n−1. The stated meiosis-II error: two normal, one n+1 and one n−1.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use one variation or nondisjunction model to trace an event to its products, including a boundary on the prediction.
criteria: Follow the affected chromosomes or combinations.

frames.title: Gamete development
frames.scenario: Compare a typical spermatocyte lineage with a typical human oocyte lineage in chromosome reduction and cytoplasmic allocation.
orderedExplanation: Both lineages use meiosis to reduce homologous sets.
A successful primary spermatocyte lineage produces four spermatids through relatively even divisions.
Oogenesis retains most cytoplasm in one large cell, with polar bodies, and includes characteristic meiotic pauses.
frames.conclusion: Both pathways reduce sets, but their products differ in size, developmental timing and allocation of cytoplasm. An ovulated secondary oocyte typically remains paused in metaphase II.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sources of variation
frames.scenario: Separate three sources of new combinations: crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization.
orderedExplanation: Crossing over exchanges corresponding regions between homologous nonsister chromatids.
Independent assortment changes combinations of homologues from different pairs in gametes.
Fertilization combines one gamete from each parent, adding another combination step.
frames.conclusion: These processes reshuffle existing genetic variants at different stages. Mutation is a separate source of new sequence variants and need not occur for every new combination.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Nondisjunction
frames.scenario: In a simple two-division model, homologues of one pair fail to separate in meiosis I. Compare the four gametes with a case in which sister separation fails in one meiosis-II cell.
orderedExplanation: For the meiosis-I error, send both homologues to one first-division product and neither to the other.
After normal meiosis II, obtain two n+1 and two n−1 gametes for that chromosome.
For the stated meiosis-II error, obtain two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n−1.
frames.conclusion: The distribution differs by timing: all four gametes are affected in the simple meiosis-I case, while two remain normal in the specified meiosis-II case.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Twins and early development
frames.scenario: Compare two embryos arising from one fertilized egg that later separates with embryos arising from two separately fertilized eggs.
orderedExplanation: One zygote followed by separation supports a monozygotic origin.
Two oocytes fertilized separately support a dizygotic origin.
Distinguish the origin of genetic similarity from later differences in development, environment and acquired changes.
frames.conclusion: Monozygotic twins arise from one zygote and are usually highly genetically similar. Dizygotic twins arise from separate fertilizations and have a genetic relationship comparable to other full siblings in the stated family model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does a monozygotic origin guarantee identical traits throughout life?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Development, environments and later changes can differ despite high genetic similarity.

topics.observableQuestion: How do organisms place meiosis and fertilization in different life cycles?
topics.learningGoal: Compare sexual and asexual strategies and annotate moss, pine and selected animal cycles without merging their distinct stages.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Mitosis preserves the current set number; meiosis reduces it and fertilization restores it. Haploid cells can divide by mitosis. Reproductive success depends on context.

retrieval.prompt: Name the ploidy transitions caused by meiosis and fertilization in a plant cycle.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Meiosis changes 2n to n; fertilization changes n to 2n. Mitosis preserves the current set number between them.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Compare two reproductive strategies using a specific organism, one mechanism and one environmental tradeoff.

frames.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
frames.scenario: A fictional plant population can produce runners or seeds after fertilization. Compare inheritance and one ecological tradeoff.
orderedExplanation: Runners develop through mitotic growth from the parent and usually preserve its genotype apart from new changes.
Sexual reproduction combines gametes and can reshuffle parental variants.
Compare speed, resource investment and variation in the stated environment rather than ranking one strategy as universally superior.
frames.conclusion: Asexual propagation can rapidly preserve a successful genotype; sexual reproduction can generate new combinations. Their relative effects depend on conditions, and neither guarantees survival.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Life-cycle transitions
frames.scenario: Trace a moss life cycle from a diploid sporophyte through spores, gametophytes and fertilization. Compare the corresponding ploidy transitions in pine.
orderedExplanation: Meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores.
Spores grow by mitosis into haploid gametophytes, which produce gametes by mitosis.
Fertilization restores diploidy; pine retains these broad transitions with much reduced gametophytes associated with the dominant sporophyte.
frames.conclusion: Meiosis changes 2n to n, fertilization changes n to 2n, and intervening mitosis preserves the current set number. Plant spores and gametes are different stages.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Animal strategies
frames.scenario: Compare a Daphnia model that switches reproductive modes with a jellyfish model containing a polyp stage and a medusa stage. Avoid adding a medusa stage to a sea-anemone cycle.
orderedExplanation: Identify which Daphnia conditions in the supplied model favour asexual or sexual reproduction.
In the jellyfish example, distinguish mitotic asexual production from gamete formation and fertilization.
Treat the sea-anemone example separately because a medusa stage is not part of its life cycle.
frames.conclusion: Different animals can combine reproductive strategies in different sequences. Shared vocabulary does not establish that their complete life cycles are identical.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Evidence and applications
frames.scenario: A fictional nursery compares cloned cuttings with seedlings across a stable treatment and a changing treatment. What would make the comparison informative?
orderedExplanation: Define an outcome such as survival or growth over the same interval.
Replicate groups and control starting size, care and sampling while recording the reproductive origin.
Compare variation and performance separately, then revise a claim that one method must always win.
frames.conclusion: The study can test outcomes under its stated conditions. It cannot establish a universal ranking without evidence across other genotypes and environments.

checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. The jellyfish and sea-anemone cycles must remain distinct.

topics.observableQuestion: Why can different genotypes produce the same scored phenotype?
topics.learningGoal: Use genetic notation accurately and distinguish dominance, allele frequency and environmental contributions to traits.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: A gene region can have alternative alleles. Diploid individuals carry two copies at a typical autosomal locus. A measured trait depends on a stated expression model.

retrieval.prompt: In complete dominance, which two genotypes can share the dominant phenotype?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: AA and Aa share the scored dominant phenotype while remaining different genotypes.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Correct one claim equating dominant with common, beneficial or environmentally fixed, using the relevant distinction.
criteria: State what evidence would address the other claim.

frames.title: Inheritance language
frames.scenario: In a stated one-locus model, A is completely dominant to a. Translate AA, Aa and aa into genotype and phenotype descriptions.
orderedExplanation: Define the alleles before interpreting the letters.
Identify AA and aa as homozygous and Aa as heterozygous.
Under the stated complete-dominance model, group AA and Aa by the dominant phenotype while retaining distinct genotypes.
frames.conclusion: There are three genotypes but two phenotype categories in this model. The notation does not say which allele is common, beneficial or older.

frames.title: Trait expression
frames.scenario: A fictional population contains mostly aa individuals even though A is completely dominant. Is the observation contradictory?
orderedExplanation: Use dominance to predict the heterozygote's phenotype.
Use population counts to describe allele or phenotype frequency.
Keep the expression rule separate from the frequency measurement.
frames.conclusion: There is no contradiction. Complete dominance describes expression in a heterozygote; it does not require the dominant allele or phenotype to be common.

frames.title: Genes and environment
frames.scenario: Two fictional plants share a stated genotype but grow to different heights under different light conditions. Does this disprove inheritance?
orderedExplanation: Identify the shared genotype and the changed environment.
Recognize height as an outcome that can depend on several genes and environmental conditions.
Seek a controlled comparison before attributing the entire difference to light.
frames.conclusion: The observation is compatible with environmental influence on an inherited developmental system. It does not show that genes are irrelevant or that one environmental difference is the only cause.

checkpoint.prompt: Does a dominant allele have to be the most frequent allele?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Dominance describes heterozygote expression, not population frequency.

topics.observableQuestion: How can a cross test a model of allele transmission?
topics.learningGoal: Connect segregation with meiosis, define inheritance notation and use offspring observations as probabilistic evidence.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Gametes carry one allele per locus in the model. Phenotype rules must be stated separately from genotype combinations. A small sample need not equal an expected ratio.

retrieval.prompt: What gametes does Aa predict, and with what probabilities under equal transmission?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: A and a, each with probability 1/2 across the stated gamete model.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use the four-dominant-offspring test-cross case to compare AA and Aa explanations without claiming proof from a small sample.

frames.title: Controlled crosses and evidence
frames.scenario: A fictional true-breeding AA parent is crossed with aa under complete dominance. Predict the first generation, then identify the next cross that tests segregation.
orderedExplanation: Each AA parent gamete carries A and each aa parent gamete carries a.
All first-generation offspring are Aa under this model.
Cross two Aa individuals and compare the next generation with the predicted genotype and phenotype proportions.
frames.conclusion: The first generation is all Aa with the dominant phenotype. Aa × Aa predicts 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa and, under complete dominance, 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

frames.title: Segregation
frames.scenario: Connect an Aa parent's two allele types with meiosis and its predicted gametes.
orderedExplanation: Place A and a at corresponding loci on homologous chromosomes.
Follow homolog separation during meiosis I and the later separation of sister copies.
Under the stated equal-transmission model, assign probability 1/2 to A and 1/2 to a in a gamete.
frames.conclusion: The two alleles segregate into gametes; a gamete carries one of them at this locus. The 1/2 probabilities are predictions across many gametes, not a guarantee for every small sample.

frames.title: Inheritance modes and notation
frames.scenario: A supplied model gives heterozygotes a phenotype distinct from both homozygotes. A student applies a 3:1 phenotype ratio to a heterozygote cross. Repair the prediction.
orderedExplanation: Define the three genotype-to-phenotype relationships first.
Construct the heterozygote × heterozygote genotype probabilities: 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.
Keep the three phenotype categories because the heterozygote does not share either homozygote's phenotype.
frames.conclusion: The phenotype prediction is 1:2:1 in this model. The genotype probabilities do not change merely because the expression relationship differs from complete dominance.

frames.title: Probability and test crosses
frames.scenario: An individual with a dominant phenotype is crossed with aa. Four observed offspring all have the dominant phenotype. Does this prove that the unknown parent is AA?
orderedExplanation: Compare AA × aa, which predicts all dominant offspring, with Aa × aa, which predicts 1/2 dominant per offspring.
Under independent outcomes, calculate the chance of four dominant offspring from Aa: (1/2)^4 = 1/16.
Use the observation as evidence without treating a possible outcome as impossible.
frames.conclusion: The result is more consistent with AA under the simple alternatives, but it does not prove AA. An Aa parent could produce this small sample with probability 1/16.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Do four dominant offspring from a test cross prove the unknown parent is AA?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. An Aa parent can produce that sample with probability 1/16 under the model.

topics.observableQuestion: Which assumptions make a familiar inheritance ratio valid?
topics.learningGoal: Construct mono- and dihybrid crosses, apply probability rules and compare model expectations with supplied samples.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Allele symbols and parental genotypes define gametes. Multiplication needs appropriate independence; addition of simple alternatives needs no overlap. Expected counts are not guaranteed counts.

retrieval.prompt: For AaBb × AaBb with independent loci, what is P(aaB_)?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: P(aa) × P(B_) = (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16 under the stated model.

criteria: Explain why deviation alone does not prove model failure.

frames.title: Monohybrid crosses
frames.scenario: Solve Aa × Aa under complete dominance, showing genotype and phenotype probabilities separately.
orderedExplanation: List A and a gametes from each parent with probability 1/2.
Combine them to obtain AA, Aa, aA and aa, each with probability 1/4.
Combine Aa and aA as the same heterozygous genotype, then group phenotypes by the stated dominance rule.
frames.conclusion: Genotypes: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. Phenotypes: 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive.

frames.title: Probability rules
frames.scenario: For independent loci in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance, calculate the chance of aaB_ and the chance that exactly one of two independent offspring is aa.
orderedExplanation: At the two loci, P(aa) = 1/4 and P(B_) = 3/4, so multiply to obtain 3/16.
For two offspring, the specified orders aa then not-aa and not-aa then aa each have probability (1/4)(3/4).
Add the mutually exclusive orders: 3/16 + 3/16 = 3/8.
frames.conclusion: The requested probabilities are 3/16 and 3/8. Multiplication uses the stated independence; addition combines non-overlapping alternatives.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Dihybrid crosses
frames.scenario: List gametes from AaBb under independent assortment and predict the phenotype proportions in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance at both loci.
orderedExplanation: Combine A or a with B or b to obtain AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability 1/4.
Combine the two parents' gametes in a 4 × 4 square or multiply single-locus probabilities.
Group the outcomes as A_B_, A_bb, aaB_ and aabb.
frames.conclusion: The predicted phenotype proportions are 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 under the stated assumptions.

frames.title: Testing a model

Compare proportions and sample sizes without demanding an exact ratio in each sample.
frames.conclusion: All four samples differ from exact expectations. Such differences alone do not reject the model; interpretation needs sampling variability, replication and checks on the design.
